items.title: 66095_Benny Carter oral history interview
items.q: When I arranged for Goodman ... gee ... I did mostly pop tunes

ctx.x: Right. And he still didn't have it made, you know. Studies of his career and his bands show that he still had some way to go after that, but that stresses the big phenomenon, of all the kids loving this dance music and so on.

Now what went in to that music? You were still here at that time. When you arranged for Benny Goodman in the summer, I think it was, or the Fall of 1934, do you remember that? It was around the time you went to the Music Hall. What sort of things, if you can reconstruct that, were you arranging for him? The same sorts of things you would do for your own band, which you, I think, no longer had?
Right. I no longer had the band. When I arranged for Goodman ... gee ... I did mostly pop tunes, you know, like 'It Happens to the Best of Friends' and 'I'm a Builder Upper', and ...

items.title: Carter Benny — Smithsonian Jazz Oral History
items.q: I’d like to, since we did just mention Benny Goodman, one thing you were doing in 1934, you began to arrange for his first big band.

ctx.x: But I wasn’t frantically working to keep the orchestra together, although I certainly wanted to, but frantic is not a word for me. I was always looking forward and hoping better things would happen. But no, I was not frantically working to keep it together.

You began to do some arranging outside; well, you were doing that all along, but it seems that this intensified sort of as the band began to disintegrate or as work was beginning to become more sparse. I’d like to, since we did just mention Benny Goodman, one thing you were doing in 1934, you began to arrange for his first big band.
Yeah, that’s when they were at the Billy Rose Music Hall [phonetic], before he even got the radio show. What was that show?
